title: Factorial Recursion and Return Value Propagation
concept: The return value of a recursive function propagates in reverse order through the call stack

steps.title: Including header file
steps.explanation:
We include the standard I/O library with **`#include <stdio.h>`** to use `printf`.

In this lesson, we learn the second key aspect of recursion -- **return value propagation**.

steps.title: Starting main - calling factorial(4)
steps.explanation: **`int result = factorial(4);`** -- The declaration of `result`, calling `factorial(4)`, and storing the return value are all on one line, but in reality `result` is not filled until `factorial(4)` finishes.

steps.title: factorial(4) -> factorial(3) -> factorial(2) calls
steps.explanation: **`return n * factorial(n - 1);`** -- factorial(4) tries to compute `return 4 * factorial(3)` but does not yet know the result of factorial(3). factorial(3) also tries to compute `return 3 * factorial(2)` but needs factorial(2)'s result first. This chain of deferred computations keeps building up the stack.

steps.title: factorial(1) - base case reached!
steps.explanation: When factorial(2) calls factorial(1), `n <= 1` becomes **true** -- the **base case** has finally been reached! It no longer calls itself and immediately returns the value `1`.

steps.title: Return value propagation: 1 -> 2 -> 6
steps.explanation: Return values propagate in reverse order -- the most elegant part of recursion. When factorial(1) returns **1**, factorial(2) computes `2 * 1 = 2`, then factorial(3) computes `3 * 2 = 6`, with frames being popped one by one.

steps.title: Final return: factorial(4) = 24
steps.explanation:
factorial(4) returns `4 * 6` = **24**, and the value is stored in main's `result`.

Recursion is usually understood in two phases: the winding phase where the problem is broken down going in, and the unwinding phase where the value obtained at the base case is combined going back out.

steps.title: Printing the result
steps.explanation:
**`printf("4! = %d\n", result);`** -- Prints the value `24` from `result` using `%d`, displaying `4! = 24` on screen.

To summarize how recursion propagates return values: going in, the big problem is split into smaller ones (4!->3!->2!->1!); coming out, small answers are combined to build the big answer.

quiz.question: How many times is the factorial function called in total when factorial(5) is invoked?
quiz.explanation:
factorial(5) -> factorial(4) -> factorial(3) -> factorial(2) -> factorial(1) results in a total of 5 calls.
At factorial(1), the base case is reached and no further calls are made.

misconceptions.wrong: A recursive function computes its result immediately
misconceptions.correct: It defers computation until the base case is reached, then combines results on the way back.
misconceptions.why: factorial(4) needs the result of factorial(3) to compute, so results propagate in reverse order only after all calls have completed.

misconceptions.wrong: Recursion is always slower than loops
misconceptions.correct: Simple recursion has function call overhead, but with tail recursion optimization it can achieve the same performance as a loop.
misconceptions.why: When the compiler detects tail recursion, it can transform it into a loop. However, this factorial uses the form n*factorial(n-1), which is not tail recursive.

keyTakeaway: The return value of recursion starts at the base case and propagates in reverse order through the call stack.
